title: Stop Doing crush grip Wrong: Train Your hand tendons Instead
description: Max grippers and sloppy singles have built a generation of strong-looking, tendon-poor crush grips. Here is the scale test that reads your true crush, the wrong way that stalls it, and the full-range tendon way that makes crush force real.

scenes.narration: Here is your test. Take a bathroom scale, the flat kind you stand on. Hold it in one hand, fingers wrapped around one edge, thumb around the other, and CRUSH it: squeeze the scale between your fingers and thumb as hard as you possibly can, and read the peak kilograms. That is your crush number, a home dynamometer that costs nothing. Do both hands; your score is the weaker one. Keep the number. Most men train crush exactly wrong, chasing grippers and singles while their hand tendons stay poor. At the end of this video I will show you the wrong way, the right way, and what your kilograms really say about your cables.

scenes.label: THE FORTY-KILO LINE
scenes.narration: Here is the line, on a home scale, squeezed one-handed: forty kilograms. Under twenty-five, your crush is untrained, whatever your arms look like. Twenty-five to thirty-one: the cables are waking up. Thirty-two to thirty-nine: BUILDING, a crush that holds bars, ropes and opponents with authority. Forty and beyond: WIRED, handshake-legend territory. Home scales vary, so treat this as your personal ruler across the season, not a laboratory reading. What matters is that the ruler never changes, so when it moves, you know exactly what moved it: your tendons.

Look at what a crush actually is. Each finger is pulled by TWO cables: a superficial tendon that bends the middle joint and a deep tendon that bends the fingertip, layered like ropes in a sleeve. Add the thumb's long tendon and the crush is a five-cable event, all of it powered from the forearm. There is no hand muscle doing this work; the hand is a puppet and the tendons are the strings. That is why the title of this video is literal. Crush grip is hand tendons. Train anything else and you are decorating the puppet instead of strengthening the strings. There is a reason crush is tested with a scale and not a gripper in this video. A gripper tells you which gripper you can close, a number that mixes your strength with the tool's spring, handle spread and knurling. A scale tells you force, full stop, and force is the thing your tendons actually produce. Grip sport learned this the hard way, which is why its serious athletes test on dynamometers and treat gripper brands like different sports. Your bathroom scale is a poor man's dynamometer, and used consistently, it is an honest one.

beats.title: THE PUPPET AND THE STRINGS
lines: The hand has almost no muscle for this.
Five cables do the whole crush.

scenes.narration: Now the wrong way, because it is everywhere. A guy buys a heavy gripper, clicks out sloppy singles with a half-open start, lets the handles slap shut with momentum, and calls it crush training. Three things go wrong. The range is partial, so the tendons only learn one angle. The close is ballistic, so peak force is borrowed from speed, not built by tension. And the OPENING, the negative, is thrown away, though tendons adapt most to controlled lengthening. His gripper number climbs while his scale number naps. The tool improved. The hand did not. One more wrong-way habit deserves naming: setting. Setting a gripper means using the other hand to squeeze it nearly shut before the working hand starts, turning a full crush into a partial. It has its place in gripper sport, but as your only training it amputates the exact range where your tendons are poorest. If the scale test exposed a weak full close today, the set is probably why. The right way starts every rep from a hand opened wide enough to wave with. No help, no head start, no theatre.

beats.text: THE TOOL IMPROVED, NOT THE HAND

scenes.narration: The force curve explains the fix. Your crush is strongest in the middle of the close and weakest at the very end, when the fingers are fully shut. That end range is pure tendon territory, where the cables work at their longest and the leverage is worst. The wrong way never visits it, because grippers get set from a comfortable start. The right way lives there: full closes, a one-second hold at complete closure, then a slow, fighting open. Train the end of the range and the scale number moves, because you finally trained the part of the crush that was losing. Expect the first month to feel unfair. Your gripper numbers may even dip while your hand relearns the full range. That is the sound of a shortcut being removed. By week six the scale starts paying back the honesty, with interest, in kilograms you can read.

beats.title: END RANGE = TENDON TERRITORY
lines: The last centimetre is where crush is lost.
Hold the close, fight the open.

scenes.narration: The right way has a second half nobody does: the NEGATIVE for the fingers is the opening, and the opening belongs to the extensors. After your crush sets, finish with slow band spreads, opening against resistance under control. It sounds like a different exercise because it is: you are training the cables that reset the hand and protect the elbow, and a hand that opens fully and fast crushes harder on the next rep. Wrong-way crush is a one-way street. Right-way crush is a loop, close with violence, open with control, repeat until the tendons have no questions left.

beats.title: CLOSE HARD, OPEN SLOW
lines: Full opening makes the next crush stronger.

scenes.narration: Your advantage in crush is the season's recurring gift: the scale cannot see your arms. Crush force is tendon tension, and tendon tension does not scale with bodyweight the way bar lifts do. A lean guy with dense cables and full-range training embarrasses bigger men on this test every week in grip gyms. You are not behind here. You are one honest training method away from a number that makes people ask what you weigh, and then not believe the answer.
Crush with me. Thirty seconds: full closes, one-second hold at the shut, slow fighting opens. Thirty seconds rest, four rounds. Every rep visits the end range. Go.

So here is the right way, as a checklist. Full range on every rep, from wide open to completely shut. A one-second squeeze at full closure, where the tendons are weakest and the adaptation is richest. A slow negative, opening against your own control for two to three seconds. Both hands, weak side first. Two or three sessions a week, never daily maxes, because these cables recover slower than the muscles pulling them. And one warning that outranks the rest: a sharp ache deep in a finger, or a finger that starts catching when it opens, is a tendon asking for mercy. If finger pain or catching persists, see a professional before you crush again. Do it this way and the scale becomes a progress report instead of a disappointment.

beats.text: HOLD THE SHUT, FIGHT THE OPEN

scenes.narration: So, your kilograms, weaker hand. Under twenty-five: untrained cables, and the right way will move you faster than any new gripper. Twenty-five to thirty-one: BUILDING, the strings are tightening. Thirty-two to thirty-nine: strong, authoritative crush. Forty plus: WIRED, the handshake people remember. Put your kilos in the comments, just the number. In thirty days we crush the same scale again, full range and honest, and the tendons will report what the method was worth.

Thirty days of full closes and fighting opens, and the scale will read a hand you have not met yet. Subscribe, because every week we test another cable the mirror cannot see. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
